Pion zeros, one case at a time

A picture guide to Definition 2.7, Theorem 2.9 and Theorem 3.1 of pion-completeness-A

Teaching companion, not part of the paper. It draws each kind of zero in the list \(\cG_N\) once, in the kinematic-mesh style of ACDFH's Figure 2 (every \(X_{i,j}\) and \(c_{i,j}\) labelled). Every example was checked by exact rational arithmetic (§6). Draft 2026-09-29.

  2. The whole list in one recipe
  3. Two cut legs: the causal diamonds (ACDFH)
  4. Three or more cut legs of one parity (CEU, CHZ, and the new ones)
  5. N = 12, |T| = 5: a zero that no earlier paper has

1. How to read the pictures

Each figure has two panels showing the same set of conditions.

Left: the leg circle. The \(N\) particles (“legs”) sit around a circle in their colour order \(1,\dots,N\). A filled dot is a cut leg. Cutting splits the other legs into runs, the arcs \(A_1,A_2,\dots\) (coloured bands). A line joins two legs whose invariant is set to zero. Where a figure has a dashed chord, it joins two dual points (small squares; dual point \(i\) sits between legs \(i-1\) and \(i\)). That chord is the diamond's corner variable.

Right: the kinematic mesh, drawn the way ACDFH draw it in their Figure 2:

  • every vertex is a planar variable \(X_{i,j}=(p_i+p_{i+1}+\dots+p_{j-1})^2\), the squared total momentum of the run of legs \(i,\dots,j-1\);
  • every tile is a mesh variable \(c_{i,j}=-s_{ij}=-2\,p_i\cdot p_j\) for two non-adjacent legs;
  • tile \(c_{i,j}\) has \(X_{i,j}\) at the bottom, \(X_{i+1,j}\) on the left, \(X_{i,j+1}\) on the right and \(X_{i+1,j+1}\) at the top. Going up-left adds one to the first index; going up-right adds one to the second;
  • the two dashed vertical lines are the boundaries. Their vertices are \(X_{i,i+1}=p_i^2=0\) (massless legs), shown in grey;
  • indices are read mod \(N\), and \(c_{i,j}=c_{j,i}\), \(X_{i,j}=X_{j,i}\). So the mesh repeats going up, flipped left-to-right each time (ACDFH call this the Möbius symmetry), and every tile appears twice in a window one period tall. A condition is shaded at every place it appears.

The one identity to remember
For any tilted rectangle in the mesh, \[ X_{\rm bottom}+X_{\rm top}-X_{\rm left}-X_{\rm right}\;=\;\sum_{\text{tiles inside}} c_{i,j}. \] For one tile this is just the definition of \(c_{i,j}\) (paper eq. (1)). Larger rectangles follow by adding tiles, because the inner vertices cancel. A causal diamond is a rectangle whose left and right corners sit on the two boundaries, where \(X=0\). If every tile inside is set to zero, the identity gives \(X_{\rm top}=-X_{\rm bottom}\).

Physics in one paragraph. \(s_{ab}=0\) means the momenta of legs \(a\) and \(b\) are orthogonal in the Minkowski sense. The amplitude \(\cA_N\) is a rational function of the \(X\)’s. Its denominators, the propagators, are \(X\)’s: at tree level, \(1/X_{i,j}\) says that the legs \(i,\dots,j-1\) merge into a single virtual particle. Pion (NLSM) interactions always join an even number of lines. So a virtual line has to separate an odd number of external legs from the rest, and that is why \(\cA_N\) has poles only at odd chords \(X_{i,j}\) with \(j-i\) odd (paper Facts 2.3(a)). Chords with both ends of the same parity are never poles. This parity split runs through everything below.

2. The whole list in one recipe

Every member of \(\cG_N\) (Definition 2.7) is built the same way:

  1. Cut a set \(G\) of legs. The remaining legs fall into arcs \(A_1,\dots,A_k\), with \(k=|G|\).
  2. Separate the arcs: set \(s_{uv}=0\) for every \(u\) and \(v\) in different arcs. Pairs inside one arc stay free. This set of conditions is \(S_G\) (Definition 2.6).

What changes from case to case is only which cuts are allowed:

Cut legs \(G\)Name in the paperFirst found inShape in the meshExample here (N = 8 unless noted)
2 legs, same parity\(S_T\), \(|T|=2\)ACDFHone causal diamond whose bottom corner is a same-parity chord§3.1: \(T=\{2,6\}\)
2 legs, opposite parity, both arcs non-emptyodd-chord diamondACDFHone causal diamond whose bottom corner is an odd chord (a propagator)§3.2: \(\{2,5\}\)
3 legs, same parity\(S_T\), \(|T|=3\)CEU3 blocks in the interior of the mesh; no diamond§4.1: \(T=\{2,4,8\}\)
all \(N/2\) legs of one parity\(S_T\), \(|T|=N/2\)CHZ\(\binom{N/2}{2}\) single tiles§4.2: \(T=\{2,4,6,8\}\)
\(4\le|G|\le N/2-1\), same parity\(S_T\)new here (Thm 2.9)\(\binom{|T|}{2}\) blocks§5: \(N=12\), \(T=\{2,4,6,8,10\}\)
3 or more legs, mixed paritynot in the list—same kind of blocks, but not a zero§4.3: \(\{1,3,6\}\)

A clarification worth making early
“Two legs of one parity” and “odd-chord diamond” are the two kinds of two-leg cut, not sub-cases of every \(|T|\). Once three or more legs are cut, only the same-parity choice gives a zero. There is no “odd” version of \(|T|=3\) or \(|T|=4\), and §4.3 shows the mixed-parity triple failing. So at \(N=8\) there are four kinds to draw: \(|T|=2\), the odd diamond, \(|T|=3\) and \(|T|=4\).

Why each case looks like blocks. The tiles of \(S_G\) are the \(c_{u,v}\) with \(u\in A_p\) and \(v\in A_q\). Within an arc the legs are consecutive, so \(u\) runs over consecutive first indices and \(v\) over consecutive second indices, and in the mesh that is a tilted rectangle of \(|A_p|\times|A_q|\) tiles. So \(k\) arcs give \(\binom{k}{2}\) blocks, one per pair of arcs, each outlined in the figures. With \(k=2\) the single block runs from one boundary of the mesh to the other, which makes it a causal diamond. With \(k\ge3\) every block is cut off by a cut leg on each side, so the blocks float inside the mesh and none of them is a diamond. ACDFH's rule (“a diamond reaching the boundary”) cannot see those zeros.

3. Two cut legs: the causal diamonds (ACDFH)

3.1 \(|T|=2\), same parity: \(N=8\), \(T=\{2,6\}\)

Conditions (9)
\(s_{uv}=0\) for \(uv\in\{\)13, 14, 15, 37, 38, 47, 48, 57, 58\(\}\)
In words
each of \(p_3,p_4,p_5\) is orthogonal to each of \(p_7,p_8,p_1\)
Mesh identity
\(X_{3,7}+X_{2,6}=0\) on the locus
Corner
\(X_{3,7}\): 3 and 7 are both odd, so this is a same-parity chord and not a propagator of \(\cA_8\)

The narrowest case is \(T=\{3,5\}\), where the arc \(A_1=\{4\}\) is a single leg. It says that \(p_4\) is orthogonal to every other momentum. ACDFH call this the skinny diamond and relate it to the Adler zero (§4.1 there). In the mesh it is a single line of tiles from one boundary to the other:

3.2 Odd-chord diamond: \(N=8\), cut at \(\{2,5\}\)

Conditions (8)
\(uv\in\{\)13, 14, 36, 37, 38, 46, 47, 48\(\}\)
In words
\(p_3,p_4\) are each orthogonal to each of \(p_6,p_7,p_8,p_1\)
Mesh identity
\(X_{3,6}+X_{2,5}=0\)
Corner
\(X_{3,6}\): \(6-3=3\) is odd, so the corner is a propagator of \(\cA_8\)

Same picture, different corner
In the mesh, §3.1 and §3.2 have the same shape: one diamond reaching both boundaries. The only difference is the parity of the bottom corner \(X_{a+1,b+1}\), and that is decided by whether the cut legs \(a,b\) have the same parity. The paper splits the diamonds by this because the two kinds behave differently in the NLSM:

  • a same-parity diamond is the \(|T|=2\) member of the \(T\)-separated family, and it continues to \(|T|=3,4,\dots\) (§4);
  • an odd-corner diamond does not continue. It sits across a propagator, and adding a third cut leg in the same spirit gives a mixed-parity cut, which is not a zero (§4.3).

At \(N=8\) that gives 8 skinny + 4 wide same-parity diamonds and 8 odd diamonds: the first 20 of the 30 in Example 3.4.

4. Three or more cut legs of one parity

4.1 \(|T|=3\) (CEU): \(N=8\), \(T=\{2,4,8\}\)

Conditions (7)
\(uv\in\{\)13, 15, 16, 17, 35, 36, 37\(\}\)
In words
three groups of momenta \(\{p_3\}\), \(\{p_5,p_6,p_7\}\), \(\{p_1\}\); legs in different groups are orthogonal
Source
CEU's “split kinematics” for a triple of same-parity legs (their §4.1, §4.3–4.4, from the CHY formula)

This is the smallest kind of zero that contains no causal diamond. Every diamond at \(N=8\) has 5, 8 or 9 tiles spanning the mesh, and none fits inside these 7.

4.2 \(|T|=N/2\) (CHZ): \(N=8\), \(T=\{2,4,6,8\}\)

Conditions (6)
\(uv\in\{\)13, 15, 17, 35, 37, 57\(\}\), i.e. every pair of odd legs
In words
the four odd momenta are mutually orthogonal
Source
CHZ §IV.1 (whole parity class)

4.3 Contrast: three cut legs of mixed parity is not a zero

The same recipe with the wrong parity gives no zero. That is why Definition 2.7 insists that \(T\) be “of one parity”, and why the paper can say the list is complete: Theorem 3.1(1) says that any zero like this one would have to contain a member of the list, and this one contains none.

5. N = 12, |T| = 5: a zero that no earlier paper has

Conditions (18)
\(uv\in\{\)1,3;\ 1,5;\ 1,7;\ 1,9;\ 3,5;\ 3,7;\ 3,9;\ 3,11;\ 3,12;\ 5,7;\ 5,9;\ 5,11;\ 5,12;\ 7,9;\ 7,11;\ 7,12;\ 9,11;\ 9,12\(\}\)
In words
\(p_3,p_5,p_7,p_9\) are mutually orthogonal, and each is orthogonal to each of \(p_{11},p_{12},p_1\); the three legs 11, 12, 1 are unconstrained among themselves
Why it is new
CEU covers \(|T|=3\); CHZ covers \(|T|=6\) (all even legs) at \(N=12\). \(|T|=5\) is neither, and it contains no diamond and no \(|T|=3\) set (it is minimal: dropping any one of the 18 conditions makes \(\cA_{12}\) non-zero, §6).

One picture for all T (an observation for intuition, not used in any proof)
Squeeze each arc to a single point and the cut circle becomes a \(2k\)-gon that alternates cut leg, arc, cut leg, arc, … In that small polygon, “separate the arcs” just says “all arc-points are pairwise orthogonal”, and the arc-points form one whole parity class. That is the CHZ pattern for \(2k\) legs. So

  • a same-parity diamond (\(k=2\)) is the whole-class pattern of a 4-gon,
  • CEU (\(k=3\)) is the whole-class pattern of a 6-gon,
  • the \(N=12\) example (\(k=5\)) is the whole-class pattern of a 10-gon, with one arc-point “fattened” into the run \(11,12,1\),

and each arc-point is fattened back into its run of legs, with every leg of a run individually orthogonal to every leg of every other run. Theorem 2.9 says all of these fattened patterns are zeros. The earlier papers covered \(k=2\), \(k=3\), and the unfattened case \(k=N/2\).

Counting. The same-parity \(T\) that are new are those with \(4\le|T|\le N/2-1\). That range is empty until \(N/2\ge5\):

\(N\)legs per paritynew \(|T|\)new zeros
63none (\(|T|=3\) is both CEU and CHZ)0
84none (\(|T|=3\) CEU, \(|T|=4\) CHZ)0
1054\(\binom54\times2=10\)
1264, 5\((\binom64+\binom65)\times2=42\); §5 is one of the 12 with \(|T|=5\)

So at \(N=6\) and \(8\) Theorem 2.9 adds a new proof but no new zeros. Theorem 3.1's contribution there is completeness: showing there are no others.

6. Where each example sits in the paper, and the checks

  • Definition 2.7 is the recipe of §2 with its allowed cuts: \(S_T\) for \(|T|\ge2\) of one parity, plus the odd-chord diamonds.
  • Theorem 2.9 says every \(S_T\) is a zero (§3.1, §4.1, §4.2, §5). The odd diamonds (§3.2) are zeros by ACDFH.
  • Theorem 3.1(2), minimality: each example is a zero, and removing any one of its conditions gives a locus where \(\cA_N\ne0\). Each is therefore the smallest set of its kind; the “drop one” column below checks this.
  • Theorem 3.1(1), completeness: any other zero contains one of these. For example, the odd diamond \(\{2,5\}\) plus the extra condition \(s_{24}=0\) is still a zero, but not a new one, because it contains the diamond. The mixed-parity set of §4.3 contains no member, and indeed it is not a zero.

How this was checked. \(\NLSM_N\) is computed as in Definition 2.2: the coefficient of \(\delta^{-(N-2)}\) in the Tr\((\phi^3)\) amplitude under the \(\delta\)-shift, summed over triangulations by recursion, in exact rational arithmetic. For each example we take 3 random points of the locus \(\{c_t=0: t\in S\}\) where no odd chord vanishes, and for each condition \(t\) one random point of the locus without \(t\). The evaluator reproduces the known closed form of \(\NLSM_6\). Code: surfaceology/sandbox/examples-guide/check_examples.py; this page is generated by build_examples.py in the same folder. Random points give evidence, not proof; the proofs are in the paper.

References are as in the paper: ACDFH = Arkani-Hamed, Cao, Dong, Figueiredo, He, Hidden zeros for particle/string amplitudes (figure conventions from their Figure 2); CEU = Cachazo, Early, Umbert; CHZ = Cao, Han, Zhu. See the paper's reference list.
